Now I have the full context. Let me check what the original error message was vs the new one: Looking at the changes in this PR: 1. **In `message-v2.ts` (line 600)**: The error message was changed from `"Aborted"` to `"Operation interrupted"` 2. **In `session/index.tsx` (line 1229)**: Added display of `" · interrupted"` text when the message has an `AbortedError` 3. **In `app.tsx` (line 571)**: Added early return when the session error event has a `MessageAbortedError`, preventing the toast error from showing You're right to question this. Looking at the original code, the error message was simply `"Aborted"` which is concise and clear. The new message `"Operation interrupted"` is more verbose and arguably doesn't add much value. However, looking at the full context of the PR titled "fix: cleaner interrupted experience", I can see the rationale: 1. The **main purpose** of this PR is to make the interrupted experience cleaner by: - Preventing the error toast from showing when a user intentionally aborts/interrupts an operation (the `app.tsx` change) - Showing a subtle `" · interrupted"` indicator in the message footer instead of a prominent error block 2. The message change from `"Aborted"` to `"Operation interrupted"` is more user-friendly because: - "Aborted" sounds more technical/harsh - "Operation interrupted" is clearer about what happened (the user interrupted it, not that something failed) That said, you have a valid point - the original `"Aborted"` message was perfectly fine and more concise. The change isn't strictly necessary for the PR's goal of providing a cleaner interrupted experience. The key improvements in this PR are really: 1. Not showing an error toast for intentional interrupts 2. Showing a subtle indicator in the message footer If you prefer to keep it as `"Aborted"`, that would be a reasonable change. Would you like me to revert just that message change while keeping the other improvements in the PR? **A note on granular bash command permissions** The best experience I've found for managing bash command permissions is in the Kilocode VS Code extension. When the LLM wants to execute a command, it prompts for approval and lets you choose the level of auto-approval that fits your workflow. For example, if the LLM runs: ``` bun run test -- --files=tests/browser/scenarios/errors.spec.ts --tests="Invalid checkout URL shows error" ``` You can choose to always approve at any granularity level: - `bun` — approve all bun commands - `bun run` — approve all bun run commands - `bun run test` — approve all test runs - The full command — approve only this exact invocation This approach strikes an excellent balance: it enforces meaningful permissions while letting users dial in exactly how much autonomy to grant, keeping productivity high without sacrificing control.
